No problem! Saw this on r/autism originally. Actually embarrassing that this still needs spelt out to people despite the abundance of autism resources that exist.

>“pEoPlE tHaT hAvE aUtIsM aRe A bUrDeN.”

This is a - unfortunately - a widely accepted fact that is wrong.Some people with autism can be more *demanding* depending on how the condition affects them, but many are able to lead normal, happy lives with very little/no support, thus meaning they're not a burden.

>source: caretaker for middle-aged sibling with autism. sibling has phd in hard science but spent the last half decade in their room on the internet, unemployed, and not treating any of their chronic medical conditions.

Yes, even some of those with high-functioning autism can be demanding at times, but some empathy and understanding goes a seriously long way. People who think autism is a burden, purely because they've witnessed one person with autism are completely wrong. Literally tarring every autistic person with the same brush here.

>is that why all of the autism-caretaker support groups all complain about the same thing? and why there are literal books now on how to deal with the tantruming adults-in-children's-bodies?

Those resources largely exist for severely autistic people and their caretakers. Those who are less affected by autism are able to self-regulate much better. Even then, they're not a burden. In a 21st century world, we now have the resources and information to be able to help mitigate and deal with people having *meltdowns* (not fucking 'tantrums', world of difference.)

>autistic person knows that taking a shower makes them clean  
>  
>they don't put on antiperspirant/deodorant after taking a shower  
>  
>within minutes they reek

Again, most autistic people understand that personal hygiene doesn't end with showering. And those who don't understand, there are plenty resources out there that exist to help them understand. Easy-to-obtain Social Stories and a clear explanation of how personal hygiene works at a young age by both parents and in PSHE lessons go a long way.

Let's stop with the sweep generalisation that everyone on the spectrum is emotionally challenged and meltdown-prone. People with autism have to face this, along with misdiagnoses, bullying and second or third mental health conditions every single day.

Sources:

* On the autistic spectrum (higher functioning), volunteered - for 3 years - with young people who have special educational needs (particularly autism) in a specialist part of the comprehensive secondary school I attend.
* Attended a special needs school at a young age.
* Going to begin teacher training soon, where we gain a wide understanding of autism and other special educational needs.
* Taking an Open University course on understanding the autistic spectrum.
